lines.text: Shapes and geometry surround us in everyday life, from architecture to art to nature. Two-dimensional (2D) shapes lie flat on a surface. The most basic are the circle, the square, and the triangle. A circle is perfectly round with no corners; its boundary is called the circumference, and the distance across the centre is the diameter. A square has four equal sides and four right angles (90°). A rectangle has four right angles but its sides are not all equal — it has length and width. A triangle has three sides and three angles — equilateral (all sides equal), isosceles (two sides equal), or scalene (no sides equal). Other polygons include the pentagon (5 sides), hexagon (6 sides), and octagon (8 sides). Three-dimensional (3D) shapes have depth: a sphere (ball), cube (box), cylinder (tube), cone, and pyramid are common examples. Geometry involves measuring angles, calculating area and perimeter (2D) or volume and surface area (3D). Lines can be straight, curved, parallel (never meeting), perpendicular (meeting at 90°), or diagonal. Symmetry — when one half mirrors the other — is a key concept in both mathematics and design. Understanding shape vocabulary is essential for maths, science, architecture, design, and describing the world around us.

lines.text: Most geometry terms are the same, but some differ: 'trapezium' (UK) = 'trapezoid' (US). Both countries agree on 'parallelogram', 'rhombus', and 'pentagon'. Maths (UK) vs Math (US) affects how geometry lessons are discussed.

lines.text: Pi (π ≈ 3.14159) is the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter. 'Pi Day' is celebrated on March 14th (3/14 in American date format). English speakers commonly round pi to '3.14' or 'approximately 3.14'.
